103e5a49-0d17-5f26-bb4b-53bf054167c8.title: The Basics – getting to know the Primary Colours
103e5a49-0d17-5f26-bb4b-53bf054167c8.quote: “There are not more than five primary colours (blue, yellow, red, white, and black), yet in combination they produce more hues than can ever be seen.” San Tzu

11bf29ca-c7ee-5d82-8565-1459dfae9402.title: Hue, Saturation, and Value: Visual Effects
11bf29ca-c7ee-5d82-8565-1459dfae9402.quote: “One who knows how to appreciate colour relationships, the influence of one colour with another, their contrasts and dissonances, is promised an infinite variety of images.” – Sonia Delaunay

1f017095-8e3e-52a0-b395-e5e6c5447615.title: Primary Colours and Emotions
1f017095-8e3e-52a0-b395-e5e6c5447615.presentation: The primary colours are yellow, blue, and red. The most important characteristic of the primary colours is that they are, by theory, the only three colours that are the root of every other colour and their creation cannot be achieved with the mixing of other colours. If an artist desires to have other colours on their palette, they will need to mix the three primaries to create any other colour scheme. Throughout history, primary colours have been associated with many emotions and meanings, or have been presented as symbols of peoples, nations, and deities. This practice continues to play a part in contemporary art, as well as in everyday life and culture. From the artistic perspective, artists use colour to set the tone of a piece, as well as it being an attempt to present the subject of their work in the truest likeness possible. This aids the creator in expressing his artistic vision and helps the viewer understand the composition and distinguish its contents. Therefore, the way we see numerous implementations of primary colours helps us understand what the artist wanted to depict, as well as how they wished it to be interpreted by the viewer.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d.title: Dress to Impress: Costume and Colour
3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d.quote: "Wealth and colour have been associated with each other for centuries. What does it mean if an individual wears a certain colour while others do not?"

4bb8b529-76a8-5c84-abaf-667ac043ec0a.title: Colours in Religious Art
4bb8b529-76a8-5c84-abaf-667ac043ec0a.presentation: Colour, as well as other elements within art, has always been subject to numerous interpretations and meanings. The presence of colours in religious art is no coincidence, and in all cultures and religions they carry specific connotations and symbolism. Playing an integral role in art history, religious art has proven to be an ideal source for deciphering the various symbolism colours have taken on around the world. Additionally, the colour scheme in religious art aids observers in identifying important religious characters and concepts. This is because certain characters in religious art have certain colours attributed to them which, aside from their symbolic meaning, are their so called “visual stamp” assisting viewers in following the composition of the religious scene. This all contributes to the importance of colour in religious art, where its presence is essential for approaching the viewer.

559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f.title: Carpets: A Whole New World of Colour
559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f.quote: “It didn’t even seem so far-fetched if one wanted to read the characteristics of a people from the colours of their carpets.” Ulrich Schürman, Teppiche aus dem Orient

69307149-9a81-5f2e-98a4-e58f1b2b05a3.title: The Three Dimensions of Colours
69307149-9a81-5f2e-98a4-e58f1b2b05a3.presentation: Every colour can be described as having three main attributes: hue, saturation, and value. In colour theory, hue is the degree of lightness, darkness, or any other variety of colour. Saturation defines the brilliance and intensity of a colour which can be changed depending on how much white and black (grey) are added to the chosen colour. Finally, value describes the lightness or darkness of a colour. When referring to pigments, dark values which have more black in them are called shades, whereas pigments with a greater amount of white are called tints of the given hue name of the colour. When we observe pastels or darker shades of a colour, we are actually referring to its value. When the scale of these three dimensions of colour is altered (decreased or increased) the viewer’s perspective of a work of art is also changed. These components are essential parts not only of colour theory but are also necessary in order for the perception of colour by the eye.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598.title: Jewellery and Accessories
850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598.quote: “These gems have life in them; their colours speak, say that words fail of.” – George Elliot “Jewellery tells a story without even a single word – a non-verbal communication of style.”- Michel Rosey West

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567.title: Behind Closed Doors: Private Life and Colours
a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567.quote: "I prefer living in colour." - David Hockney

cfcb0e18-9ce2-524f-b1f8-391878bc5aee.title: Beyond Natural Colours, Technical Achievement in Colours
cfcb0e18-9ce2-524f-b1f8-391878bc5aee.quote: "Sometimes, the lack of colour in art is its focal point. This section examines the technical perspective of creating colours."

d0327372-a89a-5132-9dc8-81d313ac841e.title: Colour and Wealth through the Ages
d0327372-a89a-5132-9dc8-81d313ac841e.presentation: Over time, colours in art have begun to symbolise abstract conceptions in human civilization. This refers not only to primary colours, but to secondary and tertiary colours as well. Applied and decorative arts have also fallen under the influence of colour symbolism, and its implementation has resulted in beautiful creations which serve a colourful purpose of demonstrating one’s social status and level of power. Colours started to be more associated with materials, and the possession of them was a clear indicator of financial status.  Along with fashion, the interiors of houses, villas, and palaces, as well as the objects they contain can provide important historical context and insight into the expression of status through colour and material.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365.title: Primary Colours in Architectural Monuments
dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365.quote: “Colour is a very critical thing. I’ve found that architects don’t like colour. Engineers too. And so somebody has to stand in. Because this is the finish of it. It is the emotional part of a structure.” John Hench

dde5f6b4-1f6d-5f5a-a610-354ad1697b75.title: Beyond Colours, the Monochrome of (Ink) Paintings
dde5f6b4-1f6d-5f5a-a610-354ad1697b75.quote: “Sometimes, the lack of colour in art is its focal point. This section examines the skilful effectiveness and artistic creativity that are achieved by simplex use of colour.”

ff42499d-1c90-5d25-a4a6-55ff7b917242.title: About the Exhibition
ff42499d-1c90-5d25-a4a6-55ff7b917242.presentation:
Colour represents a pivotal aspect of art. Its presence and role in art and art history has been everlasting and remains one of the most studied subjects in the art world, as well as in everyday life.  
  
The overall objective of the exhibition is to serve as a broad presentation of the role of colour in all branches of art, as well as to provide visitors with the essential terminology required for an understanding of colouristic properties. Additionally, the focus is on demonstrating how, even to the untrained eye, colours can evoke certain emotions and impressions through their vibrance and very presence.  
  
The exhibition is divided into four themes, which are further split into subthemes. Each theme takes on a certain aspect of colour. The arrangement of themes is composed in such a manner that it provides space for expansion of its contents and topics.  
  
The first theme focuses on the primary colours: red, blue, and yellow. Through the two subthemes, viewers have the possibility to get acquainted with the use of primary colours in art and architecture, their meaning, presentation and implementation.  
  
The second theme will evaluate the critical dimensions and technical achievements of colour. Through the concepts of hue, saturation, and value, viewers can get to know the huge variety of ways colour is represented, as well as seeing how the technical aspects of colour provide a completely new set of visual symbols and possibilities.  
  
The third theme’s main focus lays in the role that colour plays in the sphere of religious art. By dividing the theme into two subthemes, visitors have the opportunity to examine the symbolism of colour in various religions.  
  
The fourth theme puts focus on colour and its relation to wealth through the ages. With the aid of different artistic mediums such as painting, decorative arts, and fine art, viewers can delve into the numerous ways wealth was expressed through colourful patterns, materials, garments, and objects.  
  
The format of the exhibition, where text and image are combined, will give visitors the option to follow the textual contents through the visual examples that follow them.  
  
Another important motivation for the creation of this exhibition was its potential as a resource for students, researchers, scholars, and art enthusiasts, providing them with new and useful information about all the nuances of colour through a variety of artistic mediums. Finally, it is also hoped that the exhibition will establish itself as an open platform for partners to contribute to the expansion of the themes and subthemes, in order to continue nurturing the cross-border cooperation that MWNF has been fostering since its establishment.

103e5a49-0d17-5f26-bb4b-53bf054167c8/ab3.contextual_description: This artefact encapsulates how the colour red can be used as an intensifier, with added green details. This is a deliberate choice of the painter who wanted to draw attention to the figures which are pivotal for the understanding of the historical scene.

103e5a49-0d17-5f26-bb4b-53bf054167c8/aa2.contextual_description: Depicting a tragic story from Roman history, the red cloth around Lucretia’s nude figure creates a visual contrasts which further contributes to the dramatic nature of the scene and artistic climate of the time. Moreover, the intensity of the red compliments the light and cold tones that make up the rest of the painting.

103e5a49-0d17-5f26-bb4b-53bf054167c8/31b.contextual_description: This is another great example of blue being used to depict the heavens. Due to blue’s vast shade range, the possibilities that the colour posed for artists was almost limitless, especially in the arena of illusionism in Baroque paintings and architecture. In this piece the colour has been used to illuminate the various angelic figures. Due to the unifying blue of the painting’s background, the viewer can gaze upon the heavens from side to side with no disruptions.

103e5a49-0d17-5f26-bb4b-53bf054167c8/f5f.contextual_description: The Baroque period is well known for its vibrant use of colours and dramatic effects. This painting stands out for how it uses the blue colour of the sky, along with yellow beams representing God’s presence, to signal to the viewer that this is a scene of lamentation and distress, further verifying the dramatic nature of the artistic period.

103e5a49-0d17-5f26-bb4b-53bf054167c8/ce9.contextual_description: The blue cape and white shirt of St. Januarius draws attention to the dangerous animals that are attacking him, and the yellow hues in this painting that make up St. Januarius’s skin tone add to the anxiety that is felt in this scene. This again indicates the multitude of meanings yellow carries across canvases, as well as time.

103e5a49-0d17-5f26-bb4b-53bf054167c8/e0a.contextual_description: This is a clear example of how the colour yellow is used to depict those who are ill and plague ridden. Each figure in this painting has a yellow hue to their skin. This is because, despite the fact that yellow is widely associated with rebirth and the divine through gold, this colour is frequently reminiscent of illnesses of all kinds.

103e5a49-0d17-5f26-bb4b-53bf054167c8/45b.contextual_description: The combination of the white surfaces with its blue decorations, that include mosaics and tile work, makes this place of worship stand out from its surroundings. In addition, the choice of blue resembles the sky above, as well as the symbolic properties the colour carries in Islamic culture. This colour choice conveys to the viewer that the mosque is a holy space close to the heavens.

103e5a49-0d17-5f26-bb4b-53bf054167c8/0d3.contextual_description: Similar to the Qarawiyyin Mosque, the monument captures attention with its bright green trim that compliments the neutral colours of the structure’s walls. The green signifies an air of wealth that differentiates the monument from a mosque, marketplace, or residential area. Without this colour choice the viewer would be unaware of its significance.

103e5a49-0d17-5f26-bb4b-53bf054167c8/07e.contextual_description: The intended purpose of this carpet was for it to be placed in a private room where the owner could sit and relax with close friends. This sentiment is expressed through the lavish floral design of the carpet and the bright colours that are incorporated into its pattern. The choice of the colour red in this carpet stands out because it emphasis the lines from Persian poet Hafez that decorate its sides. By using red, the romantic nature of Hafez’s poetry is brought to light.

103e5a49-0d17-5f26-bb4b-53bf054167c8/54f.contextual_description: What is notable about this vase is that its surface is primarily covered in dark coloured paint/glaze. In the center of the vase is a portrait that is full of soft colours, such as blue and pink. The presence of softer and brighter colours, in contrast to the dark body of the vase, creates a contrast which allows observers to fully grasp the beauty of the object.

103e5a49-0d17-5f26-bb4b-53bf054167c8/6c3.contextual_description: The variety of colours in this coat is indicative of how this was a luxury item of its time. The brightly coloured fabric made of reds, blues, yellows, and greens was imported from Syria, and the patterns on them swow an evident Ottoman influence. The number of colours and quality of fabric indicate that the coat was owned by a prominent and wealthy figure, probably reserved for special occasions.

103e5a49-0d17-5f26-bb4b-53bf054167c8/1a4.contextual_description: Similar to the Dura’ah coat, this Indian dress represents what wealth and style looked like outside of Europe. The status of the wearer is being demonstrated through the numerous colours used in this garment. Although, it should be noted that by having vibrant colours this garment is also a representation of the wearer’s distinct personality.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/be8.contextual_description: The colour blue (al-azraq) in Islamic tradition often signifies the impenetrable depths of the universe, and turquoise blue is thought to have mystical qualities. Along with geometric and calligraphic motifs, the intensity of the turquoise shade brings the prayer niche to life, further contributing to the symbolism of what the mihrab is supposed to represent.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/d82.contextual_description: The spandrels on either side of the chimney hood are made of white arabesques set on a turquoise background, dark-blue arabesques, demonstrating European influence by being set on a white background, and two large ceramic bosses. A band of cartouches at the top of the fireplace arch, one on each of its seven facets, contains inscriptions with the names of the 'Companions of the Cave' and their dog, which are characters from a parable from the Quran. This again indicates the tight relation between Islam and the colour blue, and especially turquoise.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/8c3.contextual_description: The church of St. Lourenço de Almancil in Portugal is an exquisite example of the use of the famous azulejo tiles, which are characterized by vibrant colours and patterns. Also, these particular examples come from different influences, particularly the presence of Dutch tile painters who had resided in Spain, which found their inspiration in Chinese porcelain, notable by its white background and blue figures and shapes.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/23d.contextual_description: As much as the famous azulejo tiles played an important part in the interiors of churches and homes, they enjoyed equal importance in the external decoration of buildings as well. The façade is covered with plain blue azulejos (tile panels) and is further elaborated with stucco decoration around the window frames and doorways.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/c8f.contextual_description: Since the 16th century, tiles have been used in Portugal to decorate churches, palaces and gardens; in the first half of the 18th century the most sophisticated colour used on tiles was cobalt blue. Apart from depicting elaborate design patterns, these blue tiles were also painted as parts of larger compositions, creating a whole new image when put together. Designed to create the ambiance of a splendid welcoming ritual for those visiting the palace, all three characters exhibit magnificent Baroque outfits: the fabric of the jackets are embroidered with gold thread.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/c06.contextual_description: The delicacy and detail of the tile painting techniques paved the way for artists to create almost any kind of scenery or environment.  Depicting a scene from the hagiography of St. Francis of Assisi, the composition is created from smaller tiles which have individually been painted and subsequently put together to create a larger image. The nuanced use of various shade   s of blue set against the white surface of the tiles creates additional ambiance and illusions of perspective.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/742.contextual_description:
In Christian symbolism, red stands for charity and love. Sometimes, it would be used in architecture to symbolize the blood of martyrs or Christ’s blood.  
Built in brick and stone and finished in red, the church of Sao Paolo Maggiore emits a certain grandeur. The use of brick was frequent in Renaissance and Baroque architecture, and therefore we are witness to a large number of red-ish coloured buildings across the territories where these movements flourished.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/015.contextual_description: The Pena Palace in Sintra has always been a colourful fascination for tourists and researchers alike. Drastically renovated in the time of Romanticism, it was the period during with the palace also acquired its peculiar colours and represents the pinnacle of this artistic movement in Portugal. The palace incorporates architectural references displaying Manueline and Moorish influences that together produce a surprising scenario recollecting “a thousand and one nights.” Therefore, we are presented with an amalgamation of influences in terms of architecture and colour, creating a multifaceted cultural masterpiece.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/e24.contextual_description: In Islam, red symbolizes the life force. As it appears frequently on flags of many Islamic countries, it is a colour we frequently connect to the Islamic religion, as well as Muslim countries. Attracting a degree of fascination, the colour red is also commonly accompanied by green surfaces in its surrounding, implying the importance of nature and gardens in Islamic religion.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/1ea.contextual_description: Yellow is one of the most prominent colours of the Baroque period, regardless of its location. In Italy, the majority of villas, homes, and churches were painted in the vibrant colour, representing splendour, richness and status due to yellow’s resemblance to gold. Due to its frequent use, there even exists a specific shade of yellow that is in direct reference to the houses and villas painted in Tuscany, carrying the name Tuscan Yellow.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/065.contextual_description: Presenting the pinnacle of Umayyad architecture, the Dome on the Rock also represents an ideal example of color use in Islamic art. Harmonizing the influences of Byzantine,  Sassanian Persian, and Christian art of Syria, the Dome on the Rock has created a individual visual identity that does not only refer to architectural forms and mosaics, but also in regard to colour. The golden dome has become a visual stamp for the city of Jerusalem, as well as a symbol of the holiest Islamic building in the great city.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/430.contextual_description: Whilst the presence of blue and white is of great importance for Islam, it is also an essential visual signature of Judaism. Not only are blue and white the official colours of the Israeli state and a visual signifier of the Jewish people worldwide, they are also an important colour combination in the religious sphere  of Jewish identity. Namely, the variety of blue colours in Hebrew are called Tekhelet – blue-violet, blue, or turquoise dye highly prized by ancient Mediterranean civilizations.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/86a.contextual_description: Azakhana-e-Zehra was built in the Qutb Shahi architecture style. It has impressive outer elevations, and the interior of the structure is magnificent. The white exterior draws attention to the magnificent turquoise doors and domes, which ideally represent the tradition of mixing these two colours in Islamic culture.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/d5b.contextual_description:
Yellow symbolizes light which in turn is a symbol of the presence of God. Yellow is a predominant colour choice for many churches, particularly ones created in the Baroque period on the territories of Austria, Hungary and Germany. The use of yellow is also an effect of the frequent use of the color by the Habsburg family, which associated this colour with status and elite.  
Often used in combination with red, the two colors directly symbolize the presence of God, whether it be through the yellow beams of his halo, or through the blood of martyrs spilled in the name of Christianity.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/26f.contextual_description:
The colour yellow and gold are often used interchangeably throughout the Bible, allowing for plentiful interpretations. Yellow symbolizes light which in turn is a symbol of the presence of God. Yellow is a predominant colour choice for many churches, particularly ones created in the Baroque period on the territories of Austria, Hungary and Germany. The use of yellow is also an effect of the frequent use of the color by the Habsburg family, which associated this colour with status and elite.
