dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/ea2.contextual_description: MAIN 7	 	The colours yellow and gold are often used interchangeably throughout the Bible, allowing for plentiful interpretations. Yellow symbolizes light which in turn is a symbol of the presence of God. Due to this popular belief, a large number of ceilings of churches are decorated either with yellow or gold ornaments or stucco, or completely coloured in it (under the condition that there are no frescoes in the upper area of the interior of the church), resembling the glorious light of God’s divine light and halo. In Spain and Portugal, where there was a substantial Islamic influence in the arts, especially Mudejar, there are many instances where we can see Mudejar architectural elements (Muqarnas) coloured in yellow to correspond to the other elements within the interior of the churches.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/1eb.contextual_description: The rosette is a common architectural element which can be found in multiple cultures. The rosette is always in a circular form, and their real beauty comes from the clever elaboration that takes place within the circles themselves. The choice of decoration and colour of the inside of the rosette depends on the culture, influences and local preferences.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/af0.contextual_description: The beauty of the rosette is in its simplicity, and therefore its repetition in buildings is an ideal pattern for any architectural façade or interior decoration, like this niche here. It is further embellished by geometrical decorations, fine inscriptions, quotes from the Holy Qur'an and inscriptions documenting the names of the builder, designer and patron.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/669.contextual_description: Fresco decoration poses as a divine addition to the complex and elaborative architectural elements which decorate the interiors and exteriors of buildings. The imagery within the niche portrays a figure, executed in black and red watercolours against a white background using the fresco technique.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/e9d.contextual_description: Through tiles we also witness the development of various styles in art, using different colours and materials to decorate interiors and exteriors. This is a fantastic examples of the cuerda seca technique, which allowed for the production of multicoloured glazed tile decoration quickly, efficiently and cheaply. It is painted in a typical colour scheme of dark blue, turquoise, white and yellow. Muqarnas elements such as this one were produced in modular units and later set into place on building façades.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/119.contextual_description: Stucco decoration played an integral role in Baroque architecture. Due to its flexibility, stucco gives the opportunity to create all possible shapes and objects. It also helps enhance the divine frescoes or paintings it surrounds. Furthermore, stucco can be finished in any colour imaginable, yet is usually in white so as not to obstruct the colour schemes of the buildings.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/5d7.contextual_description: Tiles play an important role in architecture and interior design. Tile decoration is something that has always characterised Islamic art, and we can find them across mosques, public spaces and fountains, as well as private estates and homes. Their greatest trait is, of course, their colourful variety, which gives life to any space where they are used. This panel shows the Iznik potters at the height of their artistic prowess. A cloud-band of deep red undulates through a field of blue flowers and green leaves, all carefully organised around spiralling arabesques. The dark-blue of the border is offset by the green and red of the alternating flowers and leaves. While the form of the panel is a common one, known as a standard feature of Ottoman architectural decoration, the quality of decoration makes this a particularly splendid example.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/b2a.contextual_description: Following a similar pattern, the spandrels of the arch are filled with red and white arabesques on a dark-blue background, while the space beneath contains a masterful composition in which naturalistic flowers and large-scale arabesque motifs cleverly fill the brilliant white space without overcrowding it.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/2ca.contextual_description: The thuluth script is often favoured for ornamental calligraphy in tile work thanks to its monumental letter proportions and curvaceous painterly quality. In this example, bright green is used for the background of the peripheral panels while a dark-blue dominates the central panels. Both the floral ornamentation and the calligraphic inscriptions are coloured white and carefully stencilled in black. The spaces surrounding the inscription, as well as the space between the words, are filled with finely executed stylised vegetal motifs.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/f29.contextual_description: Apart from being an elaborative decorative element, tiles were also used for inscriptions, especially with calligraphic symbols. Founders, donators or artists who worked on buildings would inscribe dates and names on tiles and implement them into the bodies of the building, to serve as a testament of the people involved in its creation. This emphasizes the duality of tiles, of both beauty and utility at the same time.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/8c6.contextual_description: This small sample of zellij facing is testimony to the finesse and colourful magnificence of the famous panels with which the walls of the Badi Palace were covered. Thin lines alternating between blue and black spread from a centrepiece consisting of a 16-pointed star surrounded by a black fillet to form a large cross shape delimited by black knotwork, inside which there is a myriad of small white twinkling stars. Other yellow-ochre, blue and black knotwork lines branch out from this figure to make other larger compositions and star motifs that extend to the edges of the panel.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/9f2.contextual_description: These tile fragments are from the mausoleum of Buyan Qulï Khan in Bukhara. The turquoise glazed tile is decorated with an intricate vine pattern in white. The ornament is not painted but cut as a relief into the clay using a complex technique. This is a great example of how the craft of tilemaking is one with many facets, and can be executed in various techniques to create a variety of different outcomes.

dc677af8-ab22-5a45-aa49-655d978e7365/871.contextual_description: Buildings in Isfahan, capital of the Safavid dynasty in the seventeenth century, were lavishly decorated with tilework. An innovation of this period, found in palaces and other secular structures, was the use of individually painted square tiles employing the cuerdo seca technique, which were combined to form a larger pictorial scene.

69307149-9a81-5f2e-98a4-e58f1b2b05a3/ea2.contextual_description: The painting makes use of a wide variety of different hues to create a realistic depiction of a military campaign. The artist also pays close attention to the tones and shades being used on the figures and their horses, who are depicted very closely to one another, in order to create clear distinctions between them.

69307149-9a81-5f2e-98a4-e58f1b2b05a3/bd7.contextual_description: This artist has made use of highly saturated colours to create strong contrasts, which is apparent to the viewer because they stand out vividly. The brightness of these colours stresses the importance of the biblical scene portrayed in the painting. The viewer cannot help but look closely at the scene and admire the details, as well as the composition as a whole.

69307149-9a81-5f2e-98a4-e58f1b2b05a3/f05.contextual_description: This painting stands out thanks to the dark shades of blue that are incorporated into its scenery. The contrast in value from the blue colour of the soldiers’ uniform to the whitish background behind them makes this battle scene come to life. The varied dimensions of the painting’s colours make the observer feel almost as if they are actually present on the battlefield.

69307149-9a81-5f2e-98a4-e58f1b2b05a3/79b.contextual_description: Ellsworth Kelly uses nonobjective forms both in his paintings and sculptures.  In this painting, he used only two colours, red and blue of different forms. The arrangement of the two colours, which work to intensify one another, is one of the essential components of this piece.

69307149-9a81-5f2e-98a4-e58f1b2b05a3/6a1.contextual_description: This is a portrait of the wife of the painter named Ada. He presents her as a passenger in the vivid red interior of a 1960s Chevy Impala on a drive through the American Southwest. This is an example of using saturated colours of red, pink, blue and green to show a day in a life of a woman travelling on a hot sunny day.

69307149-9a81-5f2e-98a4-e58f1b2b05a3/e2a.contextual_description: Bocklin was influenced German Romantic Art of the early 1800’s. This is evident in his works with themes of death or coming danger. The painting shows a dark ruined villa, cypress trees on the right blown by the wind and a green light flickering through the scene. There was a sense of darkness at the same time sense of light creating a dreamy atmosphere. The viewer is left with many questions like if there is a storm coming or going and what exactly happened to the building.

11bf29ca-c7ee-5d82-8565-1459dfae9402/bd1.contextual_description: The hues of colour used in this painting are bright and unrealistic. With the aid of these hues, the main protagonists of the composition are brought forth. Furthermore, the unrealistic colour scheme catches a viewer’s attention and brings to light the intensity of this religious imagery.

11bf29ca-c7ee-5d82-8565-1459dfae9402/899.contextual_description: This object is special because it is painted all in the colour blue, which demonstrates the great lengths hues can achieve in one work. The predominant use of the colour blue and its hues helps viewers create distinction between characters, as well as their role within the composition.

11bf29ca-c7ee-5d82-8565-1459dfae9402/107.contextual_description: This is another example of an object with the same hues.  The dominant yellow background displays the shade range of the depicted urban setting, while the high saturation of the figures’ garments makes them stand out against the monochromatic surroundings.

11bf29ca-c7ee-5d82-8565-1459dfae9402/673.contextual_description: This object is a perfect example of a work of art with low value in its colours. This can be observed in how every shade that is present is darker in colour. There are no bright colours or pastels included, only darker hues which help create the holy nature of the image.

11bf29ca-c7ee-5d82-8565-1459dfae9402/47f.contextual_description: This object is a unique example of an artist using colours with low value and saturation. This can be noted in how the colours are similar in hue, and not one is brighter or darker than the other. The low saturation of the object is seen in how the figures and background blend together into one scene.

11bf29ca-c7ee-5d82-8565-1459dfae9402/578.contextual_description: This painting is a great example of when  colours with low value levels are used to create the illusion of space in a work of art. By giving higher value to colours in the front, the figures and elements in the upper area of the painting seem more distant than they actually are.

11bf29ca-c7ee-5d82-8565-1459dfae9402/128.contextual_description: This painting is an example of what a work of art with low saturation looks like.  All the colours appear muted and less vibrant than a viewer would expect from a battle scene. One reason for this low saturation could be that the artist wanted to depict the gravity of the chilling scene portrayed in their work. The low saturation in the painting attempts to decrease the dramatic nature of the composition, and wishes to emphasize the severity and brutality of war.

11bf29ca-c7ee-5d82-8565-1459dfae9402/6c5.contextual_description: Overall, the background of this object has low saturation in its colours. By having muted colours in the background the figures stand out more to the viewer. For instance, the blue and red these figures are wearing is more impactful when placed in front of a dull background.

11bf29ca-c7ee-5d82-8565-1459dfae9402/a0d.contextual_description: This object, by contrast, is a solid example of a work of art with high colour aturation. Through the intensity of the cloaks, drapes, and light of the figures’ skin in the foreground, the rest of the figures and elements seamlessly blend into the lighter background, yet somehow still maintain their own saturation.

11bf29ca-c7ee-5d82-8565-1459dfae9402/f1e.contextual_description: The high saturation of this work makes it visually striking, putting focus on the three main characters in the center of the composition.  In order to fully emphasize the central figures, the background and surroundings are more dull and light, resembling contours in comparison to the sharp, vibrant and  intense center of the painting.

11bf29ca-c7ee-5d82-8565-1459dfae9402/a3a.contextual_description: This is an example of art that falls under Synchronism-an art movement the artist founded to apply color theory to music and rhythm. Macdonald-Wright used saturated hues of orange and yellow for the sky, blue green for the mountains,red for the field and blue, purple and violet for the wind.

11bf29ca-c7ee-5d82-8565-1459dfae9402/26a.contextual_description: Louis is associated with the Washington Color School, a group of painters based in Washington, DC, during the 1960s and '70s. These artists tended to create large colorful compositions with repeated shapes, often using diluted paint.Number 99 is an artwork using overlapping strokes of hues of red, blue, green and violet.

11bf29ca-c7ee-5d82-8565-1459dfae9402/a4c.contextual_description: Presenting a landmark in Portuguese modernism, Eduardo Viana’s “The Revolt of the Dolls” majorly relies on the properties of colour to distinguish the forms of his composition. Along with geometric shapes and hues, Viana’s characters come to life.

11bf29ca-c7ee-5d82-8565-1459dfae9402/bf2.contextual_description: A prolific and inventive printmaker, Rivière was tremendously influenced by the novel compositional strategies, striking colors, blatant flatness, focus on line, depiction of seasonal changes, and the fugitive effects of weather in ukiyo-e, Japanese color woodcuts, that he avidly collected. This lithograph is an example how the artist varied the values of color blue to dark and used yellow to give an atmospheric feeling of the city.

cfcb0e18-9ce2-524f-b1f8-391878bc5aee/b78.contextual_description: This ceramic is known as Ru ware, and its colour reveals a lot about it: above all its Chinese imperial status, and consequent rareness. This brush washer has been executed in a distinctive pale “duck-egg” blue glaze colour, similar to that of jade, an important material in Chinese culture. According to one medieval connoisseur, it was "like the blue of the sky in a clearing amongst the clouds after rain".

cfcb0e18-9ce2-524f-b1f8-391878bc5aee/9ce.contextual_description: This pair of vases exhibit the “peach-bloom” colour resulting from incredible technical advancements in glazing. Artists learnt to carefully control the temperature of kilns in order to create these two beautiful vases.

cfcb0e18-9ce2-524f-b1f8-391878bc5aee/4b9.contextual_description: This plate is a fine example of a technique which uses carved cinnabar lacquerware. The delicate design and colour demonstrate how successive layers of lacquer were applied to the surface of the dish. The colour read was preferred for carved lacquerware since it had long been associated with good fortune in China.

cfcb0e18-9ce2-524f-b1f8-391878bc5aee/187.contextual_description: Depicting scenes of dance and music in emerald colour, the figures truly come to life thanks to the technical properties of the materials. One side of the bottle depicts a woman playing a tambourine, while the other presents a seated prince watching a woman dance. The clever use of pale outlines further highlights the content, distinguishing the contours from the rest of the surface. With the addition of the so-called monochrome glaze, the scenes, and with them the colour, become more vivid bringing to the fore the focal point of the object.

cfcb0e18-9ce2-524f-b1f8-391878bc5aee/799.contextual_description:
Many types of glazed pottery were produced during the Islamic period, one of which was a glazed ceramic painted in monochrome. The center of the plate is filled with the word Al Mulk, meaning power, sovereignty, or ownership. This word was carved into the bottom of the plate before the glaze was applied, which meant that the cobalt-blue gathered in the grooves, making the low points darker and the highpoints lighter, creating a divine shade range, and intensifying the effect of the decoration.  
Many types of glazed pottery were produced during the Islamic period, one of which was a glazed ceramic painted in monochrome. The centre of the plate is filled with the word Al Mulk, meaning power, sovereignty, or ownership. This word was carved into the bottom of the plate before the glaze was applied, which meant that the cobalt-blue seeped down and gathered in the grooves. The result of this was to make the low points darker and the high points lighter intensifying the effect of the decoration and creating divine like shades.

cfcb0e18-9ce2-524f-b1f8-391878bc5aee/1ba.contextual_description: Due to its technical properties, glass has always provided a fantastic opportunity to push the boundaries of colour  to show their full potential. This sweet stand consists of a plate with a raised, wave-pattern rim set atop a high stem attached to a smaller base, and is made of pressed glass, which is half transparent and half opal blue. This mixture of transparency and colour provides liveliness to the object, whilst also creating visual effects and a complete range of shades of blue.

cfcb0e18-9ce2-524f-b1f8-391878bc5aee/69e.contextual_description: Lithyalin glass is a creation dating back to the 18th century, and it was discovered by a Bohemian glassmaker Friederich Egermann. The process of creating Lithyalin glass consists of the glass being cut, then painted with metal oxides and finally fired to produce a marble effect. This type of glass is easily recognisable by its red colour, known as rothwelsch, or Italian red. The objects made from Lithyalin glass are amazing examples of how cutting contributes to the perceptions of colour in glass, along with creating remarkable shapes.

cfcb0e18-9ce2-524f-b1f8-391878bc5aee/f1f.contextual_description: The forms of the hand-blown bottles, cups and little jugs are simple, but their colouristic properties give them a vibrant and unique quality. Their colours are based on precious stones: cobalt blue, bottle green, turquoise, amber yellow, or rose. Apart from coming in various shapes and sizes, the immense colour palette further contributes to the magnificence and elegance of Hebron glass.

dde5f6b4-1f6d-5f5a-a610-354ad1697b75/158.contextual_description: The landscape is sealed in a dramatic brushstroke and executed using only dark ink. The ink colour unconsciously attracts the eye and draws attention to the luxuriant volume of mountains.

dde5f6b4-1f6d-5f5a-a610-354ad1697b75/562.contextual_description: A thin layer of ink wash in the background indicates the diffusion of moonlight and thus creates the meditative atmosphere of a nightly scene. The sense of soft moonlight is further intensified by being contrasted to the bamboo at the foreground.

dde5f6b4-1f6d-5f5a-a610-354ad1697b75/c36.contextual_description: Ancient Chinese artists use black ink in different concentrations to establish the scenes and motifs. In order to visually demonstrate the misty scene while solely using ink, the artist controlled the concentration of it and captured the characteristics of cloud by shaping the silhouette of the landscape with a different tonal range.

dde5f6b4-1f6d-5f5a-a610-354ad1697b75/9b6.contextual_description: The creation of sculptures requires a long period of preparatory work before being brought to life. Therefore, sculptors primarily construct drawings of their future works, to create a preliminary representation of their vision. Usually done in monochromia, sculptural preparatory drawings are subject to heavy detail, so that they rightfully follow the patterns and shapes which will later be transferred into the third dimension. This additionally demonstrates the possibilities of monochromatic works, how they can give life to objects without having to make use of other colours.

dde5f6b4-1f6d-5f5a-a610-354ad1697b75/229.contextual_description: Whilst being enclosed within a colourful frame embellished with floral and vegetative motifs, the drawing itself is outlined in black, with added line detail and some light grey shading to add depth. The narrow, vivid red line that delineates the frame further emphasises the technical skills of the talented Iranian artist when using only the mediums of black ink and shading.

dde5f6b4-1f6d-5f5a-a610-354ad1697b75/290.contextual_description: Architectural sketches are fantastic examples of how, through monochromacy and ink wash, equal detail and precision can be transferred into two-dimensional works. The monochromatic nature of the drawing aids the observer in noticing the smallest of details, meanwhile enhancing the qualities of the drawing itself, and celebrating the artist’s pristine skill for precision.

dde5f6b4-1f6d-5f5a-a610-354ad1697b75/723.contextual_description: In the world of fashion design, detail plays an integral role in its creation. For the preparation of designs, artists create sketches to have an initial idea of the design they are going to create in fabric. Naturally, these sketches are highly detail oriented, and they vary in terms of colour, depending on the preferences and visions of the designer. This particular example finely demonstrates when the priority is given to detail above the colouristic properties of the clothes.

dde5f6b4-1f6d-5f5a-a610-354ad1697b75/c77.contextual_description: The great possibilities of demonstrating details through ink paintings can be followed outside necessarily religious and artistic books. Literary works describing nature, medicine, and, in this case, artillery, prove top be great examples of artistic technique and expression throughout history. This particular page from a work called 'Book of Glory and Advantage for Those Fighting in the Holy War with Artillery and Cannons for the Glory of God’, depicts six different projectiles in a pen and ink drawing that occupies more than half of the page. Interestingly, from a cultural and historical point of view, this North-African copy is an example of European technical knowledge disseminating into the Arab world.

f12a2ac5-2f3e-5ea5-9bf3-5840abc095bc/eff.contextual_description: Calligraphy is an essential aspect of Islamic art, and this volume of the Qur’an shows how colour is also an integral part in mastering the field of writing. The frames of the text and ornaments range from blue and green, while being outlined in gold and decorated with miniature reddish dots. Each of these colours presents an important symbol in Islamic art, alluding to the religious character of the content.

f12a2ac5-2f3e-5ea5-9bf3-5840abc095bc/1b9.contextual_description: In Islamic art, it is uncommon to find figures fully depicted in this way. It is interesting to note that while the prophet Muhammad is depicted in this scene, his face is covered from the viewer. Despite Muhammad being the focal point of the work, our attention is drawn away from him by the vibrant coloured wings and garments of the mythical creatures around him.

f12a2ac5-2f3e-5ea5-9bf3-5840abc095bc/f80.contextual_description: Mi'raj is the scene of the Ascension of the Great Prophet Muhammad to the throne of Allah in Heaven. As seen in the Khamsa, Muhammad’s face is covered with a white cloth. The vibrant and strong colours of the mythical creatures draw attention from the central point of the image, whilst the deep blue background alludes to the story the image is referring to, the famous Night Journey Muhammad took from Mecca to Jerusalem.

f12a2ac5-2f3e-5ea5-9bf3-5840abc095bc/153.contextual_description: Throughout the Christian canon of religious art, archangel Gabriel is usually depicted wearing the colour red. Usually presented in the form of a waving drape or whole garment, this colour motif symbolises the importance of the archangel as a divine being.

f12a2ac5-2f3e-5ea5-9bf3-5840abc095bc/fb8.contextual_description: Throughout Christian iconography, Mary and Gabriel are frequently pictured together. This is due to their constant connection through the Bible, and the colours usually attributed to them, blue and red respectively, are clear in their regular encounters . Hence, this is another fine example of the Virgin Mary being depicted wearing the colour blue while the archangel Gabriel is wearing red. Yet, we see how both characters also have elements of colours attributed to the other which further strengthens the bond these two characters have throughout the Bible, as well as reinforcing their association with these colours.

f12a2ac5-2f3e-5ea5-9bf3-5840abc095bc/eb7.contextual_description: In religious art, colour is often used to signify specific motifs and symbols within a religion or practice. Mary, the mother of Jesus Christ, has been depicted wearing blue in all Christian iconographies. The blue of her cloak has been interpreted to represent the Virgin’s purity, symbolise the skies, and label her as an empress, for blue was associated with Byzantine royalty. This colouristic symbolism is followed in all presentations and mediums, with an occasional addition of red.

f12a2ac5-2f3e-5ea5-9bf3-5840abc095bc/c31.contextual_description: The design of this secular advertisement for perfumes is reminiscent of religious Islamic art in terms of its colour scheme and the fashion of the depicted figure. It seems that the artist found inspiration in this artistic style and used it to create a marketing campaign based around the allure of the Middle East. In that sense the spiritual imagery of Islam has been repurposed to sell a product.

f12a2ac5-2f3e-5ea5-9bf3-5840abc095bc/2fa.contextual_description: Nagarjuna, the Buddhist philosopher from southern India, is depicted on his seat of black, writhing serpents. His disciple Aryadeva sits next to him. The red and gold colour scheme signifies the peacefulness of the deities and conveys their wisdom and achievements.

f12a2ac5-2f3e-5ea5-9bf3-5840abc095bc/033.contextual_description: Colours embody symbolism in Buddhist art and tradition. In Buddhism, each of the five colours (together known as “Pancha Varna”) signifies its respective essences and is associated with a particular Buddha or Bodhisattva. Green Tara is one of the preeminent figures in Tibetan Buddhist tradition, and her colour embodies the protection from fear. The classic green colour for Thangka paintings is usually extracted from minerals and due to the complicated nature of its production is often expensive.

f12a2ac5-2f3e-5ea5-9bf3-5840abc095bc/770.contextual_description: This early bronze sculpture visually explains his power to overcome fear and obstacles, and he is adopted by Buddhists as a protector not only in India, but also in a large part of Asia. The gold stands for knowledge, enlightenment, purity, happiness, and freedom; thus bronze is perfectly suited for Buddhist sculptures.

f12a2ac5-2f3e-5ea5-9bf3-5840abc095bc/c10.contextual_description: This stained-glass artwork is an example of how abstract art can be incorporated into religion. Instead of using the colours which are usually used or expected in traditional stained-glass art, the artist used bright colours of pink, yellow, blue, green and red. Furthermore, instead of the usual saintly figures, the artist made use of geometric forms whilst cleverly maintaining the religious character of the work.

f12a2ac5-2f3e-5ea5-9bf3-5840abc095bc/de4.contextual_description: Stained glass has a long tradition in Christian art, and was able to adapt to the revolutionary changes that occurred in art history during the 20th century. Even though contemporary stained-glass artists of the period built on tradition, in no way did this prevent them from exploring new technologies and novel forms of artistic expression. The subject of the stained glass remains traditional, but the implementation and presentation fully incorporate the artistic climate of the time in terms of form, composition and colour.

f12a2ac5-2f3e-5ea5-9bf3-5840abc095bc/602.contextual_description: This painting combines both the simplified forms and large scale of contemporary Western art with elements of Hindu Culture. The mystical combination suggests the sacred harmony that results when humans show respect for animals. This invites the viewer to contemplate how one’s actions affect other creatures living on the planet alongside humans. The deep red background dominating the artwork is balanced by the white coloured creatures and the dark coloured figure at the top.

559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f/438.contextual_description: Carpet manufacturing has had a strong tradition dating back to ancient times. Workshops emerged across the world, and each of them had their own style, colour palette and preferred motifs. This is a great example of the developed Mughal style in carpentry. The architectural element (which represents the mihrab) stands out thanks to its vivid red colour, which is further emphasised by being flanked by vegetative and floral motifs of different sizes and colours, demonstrating the importance of nature as a visual component in Islamic art.

559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f/126.contextual_description: Apart from prayer rugs, similar motifs were implemented on prayer hangings. In the Qur'an, God (Allah) is likened to the presence of a lustrous lamp in a niche. Hence, lamps are often placed in niches in mosques and, similarly, they are depicted in niches on tile panels and textiles. As seen in this example, two lamps are depicted on the sides of the colour contrasting mihrab, whilst also conveying the interior of the Islamic place of worship.

559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f/5e7.contextual_description: Originating from Kerman, a region known for its wide range of designs, the craftsmen expertly utilised natural dyes in a broad colour palette and asymmetrical knots. This Iranian carpet depicts a human with the body and wings of a bird, which demonstrates a close link between God and divine protection. Colourful patterns featuring the damask rose frame the central scene, purposefully executed in earth tones representing honesty, support and trustworthiness.

559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f/b27.contextual_description: Carpets also had religious significance in the Christian world. Usually created in tapestry form, many religious figures and scenes were depicted in this medium. This example, coming from a series of 15th century Flemish tapestries known as the “Old Passion”, shows the Ascension of Christ. Through the strong detail and colour palette, this tapestry is in keeping with the traditional style of 15th century painting. However, the monumentality of the figures and the realistic, pastel-like depiction of the landscape clearly reveal the influence of the burgeoning Renaissance.

559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f/152.contextual_description: In medieval times, the immense iconographic programme of the Catholic Church was of great import for understanding the religion. This included not only Biblical figures and saints, but also legendary creatures with no religious connotations. Tapestries with religious content frequently followed the already established rules of colour from painting. Therefore, it is no surprise that here we see Mary in blue, monks in dark garments, and Gabriel in red.

559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f/27a.contextual_description: The multiple-niche prayer carpets, called saf (from the Arabic word for “row”), are sometimes improperly referred to as “family” prayer rugs. They were used in mosques where their particular design allowed several people to pray next to one another in this communal setting. This rug features five niches boldly outlined in white on an indigo and navy-blue background. By using the colours white and blue, the character of the carpet conveys a religious spirit, since these colours play an important role in Islamic religious art.

559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f/fe1.contextual_description: The background is cream white. Within the sections outlined by dark-blue borders are five mihrab niches, two of them green and three dark blue. Each mihrab niche contains mosque lamps, further indicating the religious character of the carpet. Each niche has diamond motifs in the lower area, all executed in blue and red.

559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f/5d7.contextual_description: Since there is a standardised pattern of colours used in carpet production within the Islamic world, altercations to this indicate that a local workshop was involved in the manufacturing of a carpet, as can be seen in this arrangement of multicoloured mihrabs. Here, the uneven colour areas in the mihrab field, the somewhat irregular shape of the arches, and the stylised vegetal motifs are indicative of its tribal, probably Kurdish, provenance.

559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f/1c8.contextual_description: Ghiordes was one of the major carpet-making centres during the AH 13th / AD 19th century. Both the design and colour scheme of this rug, a deep-blue niche framed with elaborate spandrels and borders, is typical of Ghiordes rugs. Blue is the colour that represents the eternal heavens, and the floral motifs around the blue niche further allude to divinity, representing the heavenly gardens.

559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f/84b.contextual_description: The carpet belongs to the traditional type of "sajada", or prayer, carpets. The rectangular frames of different patterns gradually lead to the focal point of the carpet, which is the dark blue mihrab, also symbolising the religious heart of a mosque. The choice of ornaments and motifs usually serves as a compass for indicating the origin, since, as much they are of similar nature, are portrayed differently from workshop to workshop.

559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f/133.contextual_description: The name “Gördes knot” was coined for the symmetrical knot technique that brought fame and popularity to the region’s rugs. The niche corners are decorated with two trees of life. The head band is composed of rose and rosebud motifs, wjhilst various floral motifs are used on the borders as an expression of heavenly gardens. The central red prayer niche, as the focal point of the rug, is left without any ornaments, highlighting the principle purpose of the rug.

559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f/1b3.contextual_description: Outlined on the contrasting green of the central field, the red prayer niche has a stepped arch fringe with hooks along its inner edges. Inside the niche, a floral composition encircled by 12 tiny ewers recalls the mosque-lamp motif. This mixture of motifs and colours appears with the multiple influences arriving in workshops during the 19th century, combining Ottoman styles with European art.

559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f/f41.contextual_description: As the dawn of the 20th century approached, the essential patterns of prayer rugs remained in focus, however the ways in which these were implemented was attaining a greater variety. Completely woven in yellow, the Qajar prayer rug merely hints at a prayer niche here by two diagonals that do not meet. Additionally, a pair of hands and a flower motive above decorate the wide yellow surface. This type of arrangement gives opportunity to the beholder to encounter multiple interpretations – relying on Islamic legends and myths, in regard to Fathima’s hand; or simply seeing a visual instruction for the proper usage of the prayer rug. Either way, the hand is a common motif on prayer rugs across the Islamic world.

559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f/022.contextual_description: A version of 17th century Ottoman Turkish prayer rugs very popular in Hungary was the "column" rug, in which the mihrab (prayer niche) is divided into three fields by three, four or eight columns. This type of rug is also known as Ladik. The two main ornamental aspects of these rugs are Lilly-like motifs and the columns which are supposed to imitate the interior of a mosque. Apart from bright red and deep blue, it is the yellow in particular that dominates the carpet due to its intensity.

559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f/b60.contextual_description: It would be difficult to discuss the amazing world of carpets without mentioning the craft itself. Beginning in the Neolithic age, it is a craft that has survived all industrial and technological revolutions. To this day, therefore, carpet making represents one of the crucial crafts which connect communities, cultures and art across time and space.

559b1c48-b8c9-5d02-b05c-2bf798c9222f/c35.contextual_description: Knowing how carpets are made is of equal importance as knowing where they come from and what they are used for. An important center for the creation of kilims in the Western Balkans was Pirot, Serbia. Pirot kilims were woven on vertical looms (as the one shown in the picture) with a slit weave technique (klečanje), which renders both front and back of a weave even and identical. It took one to ten weavers to weave a kilim, depending on its dimensions.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/cf3.contextual_description: This painting shows a marketplace that serves a wide variety of different people from diverse backgrounds. What stands out is the building in the background that contrasts with the colourful figures in the foreground. This draws attention to the building as a place of worship.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/8ab.contextual_description: This painting provides a fascinating insight into the activities that took place within the Grand Bazaar of Istanbul during the 19th century. Since the famous bazaar in Istanbul is known for the variety of products that pass through it, the painter wished to embody this abundance through bright colours, along with diverse shapes and sizes. Also, through the employment of a clever colour scheme, we see a clear distinction between servants/servers and customers.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/b58.contextual_description: Another fine example of the social and colourful diversity of bazaars is the painting of the Athens Bazaar, painted by Irish topographer Edward Dodwell. Through his travels, he managed to cover a wide range of Greek subjects and record them faithfully in both his drawings and his descriptions of various aspects of Greek life and customs. With the aid of his descriptions, we can make clear distinctions between the characters in his drawings, which he also distinguishes by the colour of their outfits, as well as the type of garments they are wearing.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/1ab.contextual_description: Genre scenes are a great example of depicting multiple characters from multiple classes. It is through these scenes that we acquaint ourselves with how people from different social backgrounds dress. Here we see a mixture of different ages, classes and genders, each group of people telling their own story. The use of colour here is a compass to navigate the diversity of characters depicted in the genre scene.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/369.contextual_description: In cultures around the world, certain colours have always been favoured above others. In India, red is a popular choice, as it is thought to signal future success and prosperity. The fine red wedding saris, donated by Anjali Bulley, (nee Raval), is a vivid example. The gharchola sari is beautifully decorated with tie-dyed elephants and peacocks, which are symbols of good luck.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/152.contextual_description: Moroccan caftans represent an integral part of Moroccan wear, playing a central social and symbolic role in life’s milestones within Moroccan society.  Whether it was the ritual of birth, first fasting, circumcision, and marriage, its heritage value and distinctive character reflect its role in collective representations and the transmission of norms and practices associated with major rites of passage. During these celebrations, the caftan is considered a "meaningful garment" that through its material and aesthetic characteristics, expresses a form of continuity of ancestral practices and affirms belonging to the group. Beyond its visual elegance, the caftan functions as a powerful tool of non-verbal expression, reinforcing shared values and societal norms that are central to Moroccan identity.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/068.contextual_description: Here we see the famous entari dress, which is a term that varies from region to region within the territories of the former Ottoman Empire, but in general signifies a long dress-like garment. Traditionally, the entari was worn in the same way both on special occasions and in daily life. The only difference was in the material that was used. This bridal outfit is made of turquoise satin embroidered in various stitches using silver-gilt thread and completed by a matching hırka (long jacket) made from the same fabric and lined with red fox fur and matching heeled shoes with uppers of the same fabric and soles made of leather. The softness of the turquoise colour here emphasises the beauty of purity of the bride to be.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/269.contextual_description: The kimono is the national dress of Japan. Kimonos are simple, straight-seamed garments. They are worn wrapped left side over right and secured with a sash called an obi. The kimono’s colour, pattern, and material say a lot about a person’s social status, identity, cultural sensitivity, and more. Colours have strong metaphorical and cultural meanings. Dyes are seen to embody the spirit of the plants from which they are extracted meaning that any medicinal property is also believed to be transferred to the coloured cloth. Blue, for example, which derives from indigo (ai), is used to treat bites and stings, so wearing blue fabric is thought to serve as a repellent to snakes and insects.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/9eb.contextual_description: Traditional wedding wear has equally been a representative of social status, especially in regard to colour and origins of the materials. Traditional Palestinian costumes are characterized by strong emphasis on decoration and colour and are designed from the finest and most expensive fabrics, as shown by this dress. The vivid colour palette, consisted of yellow, red, purple, and blue, further contributes to the rich character of the wedding garment.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/4f6.contextual_description: Orientalism played a crucial role in the artistic exchange between East and West in the 19th century. A common motif in these paintings was the one of women, especially in oriental costumes. Through pastel colours and gentle tones, which allude to the transparency and light weight of the material, the painter tries to bring us closer to understanding the fashion of the time. Through the rich, detailed, and colourful interior which fills the background, he introduces us to the social status of the depicted woman.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/cb3.contextual_description: Traditional costumes in the Balkans vary from region to region, yet they were easily distinguishable by their colours and patterns. Traditional costumes were composed of multiple segments, and they were worn depending on the occasion, but also in regard to financial and social status. Here, we see a full ensemble of the traditional costume originating from North Macedonia, where vibrant colours and silver and golden tokas (coins) indicate the quality of production, as well as financial ability to purchase them. The white veil with richly decorated hair pieces suggests that this traditional costume is intended for a wedding.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/fda.contextual_description: Slippers have a long tradition in Ottoman and Turkish culture, and have always presented an essential item in households, as well as a clear indicator of the wearer’s social status. This could most easily be seen through the materials and colours of the slippers, which differed from region to region, based on their availability. This particular type of slipper is known as the Çarik and is characteristic for its pom pom like ornament on the tip of the shoe. The pair is of white and blue satin with the surface partially covered in yellow silk and are adorned with gold sequins and yellow tassels.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/d18.contextual_description: Traditional Palestinian costumes reflect complex social systems that express the owners’ social status, wealth, region and origins through different designs and decorative elements. Made of white cotton and silk with red, green, and thin, dark blue stripes, this traditional Palestinian dress represents an ideal example of a upper class dress, along with representing vivid colours that resemble the Palestinian flag.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/7ef.contextual_description: This example comes from Europe, demonstrating the evident influence Eastern fashion had on European craftsmen. Handcrafted and embroidered by hand, the slippers follow the colour scheme and ornaments that were standard at the time of production. Also, it demonstrates the fascination with oriental art in Europe during the 19th century.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/a64.contextual_description: Purple has commonly been associated with royalty, especially during the Byzantine Empire and its connection to mineral porphyry. Despite from its royal connotation, purple velvet made its way on to the slippers far away from court walls – its connection to luxury and royalty made them a popular item among many layers of society.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/b1a.contextual_description: This type of cap is called an araqiyeh, and it is customary for the people of Hebron and the surrounding villages. It is notable for its circular shape and the dangling decoration that is attached to it, usually in the form of coins or hair bands, which come in a variety of colours.  The two multicoloured hairbands (laffayef) on this araqiyeh, together with the thin black ribbons fixed to either side of the cap, are modern replacements. This headdress was made for everyday use.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/683.contextual_description: Headdresses like this one were worn by married women, as silver was the most common jewellery, as well as the most common choice of material for heavily decorated head pieces. Ottoman and Russian coinage reflects the social and economic situation of Jordan between the end of the 19th century and the early 20th century, when it was part of the Ottoman empire, and it was influenced by population movements, demographic changes and trade with distant countries. These influences are further noticeable through the variety of patterns and colours on the headband.

3062d0eb-92a1-5c62-8e39-26f7ee95395d/fae.contextual_description: Bridal traditions vary from culture to culture, and so do the colours that accompany them. The main fabric of this wedding dress is linen embellished with silk selvedge stripes, with red and yellow taffeta inserts in the sleeves and skirt; the chest panel is couched with gilt cord and yellow, green and purple silk cord, and filled with multi-coloured stain and herringbone stitches. This object testifies to the diverse population of Jordan at that time, through personal attire, fashion, local costumes and rites.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/142.contextual_description: Apart from the objects themselves, an important representation of jewellery belonging to a certain period can be found in other branches of visual culture, particularly painting. By depicting for the most part the higher echelons of society, who symptomatically had the finances to purchase more extravagant and rich pieces of jewellery, artists of the time paid particular attention to these details. This was in order to convey as much visual information about the subject of their portrait as possible. In doing so, they were also providing us with a record of contemporary trends and revolutions in fashion of the jewellery industry, as well as the personal preferences in terms of colour and material of people at the time.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/8e3.contextual_description: Apart from the objects themselves, an important representation of jewelry of a certain period can be found in other branches of visual culture, particularly painting. By depicting usually higher members of society, who symptomatically had the finances to purchase more extravagant and rich pieces of jewelry, artists of the time paid particular attention to these details in order to give out as much visual information about the subject of their portrait. Meanwhile, they were also presenting us with the current trends and fashion of the jewelry industry, as well as the personal preferences of people at the time. In this particular case, we see a rich headpiece mounted with diamonds, along with matching earrings. Diamonds are, in terms of colour, almost always considered to be white or grey, and therefore their meaning tends to change across cultures.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/593.contextual_description: Archers wore thumb rings made of semi-precious stone on the thumb of their right hand to help them draw their bows. As archery was considered a sport reserved for the higher levels of society, the materials used to create them were usually expensive and precious, a further indication of the social status of the wearer. Made of nephrite (which also falls under jade) and encrusted with rubies and gold, this archer ring embodies the ideal symbols of high society and the rich colour palette that decorated it.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/a78.contextual_description: Another fine example of an archery ring, but this time decorated in enamel, demonstrating the variety of motifs and colours that could be found on their surfaces. Depicting vegetative and floral motifs, the multicoloured decoration brings the object to life, providing it with liveliness and beauty.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/902.contextual_description: The presence of blue gemstones in jewellery is common among all cultures, civilizations, and periods. Within the vast category of blue gemstones, turquoise stands out for its beautiful light blue colour, easily catching the eye’s attention. Known as the official gemstone of the grand Persian Empire, the implementation and presentation of turqioise was frequent, whilst it was also used to resemble the beautiful blue skies and heavens.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/3ed.contextual_description: Tiaras have always been the most evident visual symbol of royalty. Typically decorated with a large amount of precious metals and stones, royal headpieces are delightful examples of the social, financial and cultural standings of their bearers and their nations/countries. Gold mostly carries similar symbolic meaning across all cultures, and has always been associated with the divine making it an essential component of headpieces produced for royalty or nobility.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/307.contextual_description: Jade comes in a variety of colours, among which the most prized are green, pink and yellow. One of the other common colours in which jade appears is white. It is usually attributed with calmative powers and nobility, and therefore it was widely used for bracelets and pendants but was not strictly limited only to that purpose.  White, considered the purest colour in Islam, further indicated the importance of white precious stones and their use in jewellery making, especially when they were inscribed with verses of the Quran, or names of rulers and their children.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/476.contextual_description: Chinese culture considers jade to be a lucky stone and each colour of jade holds a specific auspicious meaning. The green jade refers to heaven and power. In the form of a belt buckle, it thus gained the dignitary’s favour.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/f74.contextual_description: The technique of enamelling is a widespread jewellery technique practised across the world. Apart from being a great alternative for precious gemstones, enamel has the ability to, with the addition of pigments, be produced in any possible colour. Furthermore, with the use of enamel, all possible shapes could be created on the surface of the piece. For pendants and amulets, which carried significant meaning, enamel was a great material for expressing colours and scripts.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/180.contextual_description: The technique of enamelling is a widespread jewellery technique practised across the world. Apart from being a great alternative for precious gemstones, enamel has the ability to, with the addition of pigments, be produced in any possible colour. Furthermore, with the use of enamel, all possible shapes could be created on the surface of the piece. By combing green, gold and red, which are colours of great importance in Islam, this amulet provides great protection and other powers to its wearer.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/30a.contextual_description: During the 19th century, as much as other cultures were having an impact on the European jewellery scene, there was an equal influence of European trends on contemporary fashions in Islamic countries. This reciprocation of ideas was facilitated by an increase in trade and cultural exchanges. The production and wearing of jewellery of European influence indicated status and cosmopolitanism among civil society in Islamic countries. In terms of colour, we must consider that most of the pieces made in the 19th century (a period which witnessed the rise of the educated bourgeois class, so called citizens), were made with the intention of status representation than rather carrying any mystical or symbolic meaning.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/f03.contextual_description: During the 19th century, as much as other cultures were having an impact on the European jewellery scene, there was an equal influence of European trends on contemporary fashions in Islamic countries. This reciprocation of ideas was facilitated by an increase in trade and cultural exchanges.  Following similar patterns, jewellery found in the Islamic world of this period, especially secular jewellery, is quite identical to its European counterpart. The presence of diamonds, an evidently visual symbol of luxury and social status, was a common material used in these pieces, along with gold, further indicating the various stratas within civil society.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/d2a.contextual_description: Amulets are commonly accepted as objects which carry significant powers or protection to its wearer. Unanimously accepted as the most precious metal in Islam (but also in other religions), gold was a frequent choice for the production of objects which carried religious, symbolic, and magical meanings, so as to to enhance their power. These objects potency were further amplified by verses from the Quran.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/c6c.contextual_description: The production of other objects in precious metals and stones has been a known practice since ancient times. Their direct purpose may have seemed different than jewellery, yet the symbolic purpose stayed the same. Precious objects such as these came in all sorts of colours, depending on the availability, but also the specific symbolism and prestige attached to gemstones in different cultures. In Mughal culture, emeralds, the ultimate green gems, were widely praised and considered as important gems for special occasions. Highly represented in the Mughal court, emeralds were used for the creation  of a plethora of objects, ranging from headpieces and jewellery to interior décor.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/300.contextual_description: In Mughal culture, vivid green emeralds were highly praised and were considered as important gems for special occasions. In the records made by court biographers, there are frequent mentions of the gifting of emeralds for important moments in the lives of the emperor’s children and subordinates, such as birthdays, military deployments, or new governorships. Being that all Mughal emperors were of the Islamic faith, the presence of green gemstones in the royal court comes as no surprise.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/245.contextual_description: The production of other objects in precious metals and stones has been a known practice since ancient times. Their direct purpose may have seemed different than jewellery, yet the symbolic purpose stayed mostly same. Almost all precious gemstones have attributions which are health related, and therefore objects associated with health and cosmetics were often adorned with them. This, along with gems’ aesthetic properties, further alluded to the concepts of beauty and health. In the case of the red rubies, which lavishly flank this perfume bottle, they are symbols of love and passion.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/550.contextual_description: With the establishment of the World Exhibitions in the 19th century and colonial campaigns, European jewellers had an immense pool of visual influences and sources of inspiration for their magnificent creations. Using floral and other natural motifs was a common practice of this time,  with a particular emphasis on in vogue designs imported from other cultures. For a brief period, the motif of scarab beetles was a very popular choice, especially since this was near the time of the completion of the Suez Canal. These pieces followed the realistic colour scheme of these insects, usually being produced in gold or any precious stone that resembled their colour in real life, such as brown, dark yellow, dark orange, etc.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/8a8.contextual_description: Enamelling is a widespread jewellery technique practised across the world. Apart from being a great alternative to precious gemstones, enamel has the ability to, with the addition of pigments, be produced in any possible colour. Furthermore, using enamel allows the jeweller to create all possible shapes on the surface of the piece. It also has the advantage of bringing the object and its other components to life by creating contrasts in colour and shape. Even though the pigments used for enamel were usually imported, the importance of the colour had local meaning. Depicting fragments from an Arabic poem, the deep cobalt blue further vitalises the script.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/bb9.contextual_description: Outside of the sacral realm, the symbolism of gold is always associated with status and financial stability.  Therefore it was often the case that the gold itself that was the focal point of the piece, whilst also attempting to demonstrate the great craftsmenship required in its production. These techniques could sometimes create much greater and more beautiful patterns and shapes than pieces with simple shapes and precious stones. One of those techniques is that of filigree, as seen in this beautiful example from Syria. Gold, apart from its vibrant yellow colour which permits this technique to reach its full potential, is also technically very adaptable to it, being that it is realtively soft compared to other metals, making it easy to shape and intertwine.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/5ba.contextual_description: Inscribed precious stones were a frequent phenomenon encountered at the Mughal court. Due to their exotic origin and colour, we stumble upon a great number of examples in which verses from the Quran, or important names and dates are inscribed into the vividly green gemstone. The importance of emeralds, and symptomatically its colour, have also been mentioned in treaties and scripts, with their appearance on the market after the discovery of the Americas. One treatise, in circulation at the Mughal court, entitled Javahirnama (“Treatise on Precious Stones”) lists the numerous benefits of emeralds: it was considered an antidote for poisoning, it was believed to strengthen the heart, and it was thought to be useful against ailments of the stomach and liver as well as epilepsy. Therefore, the text states, the children of a ruler often wear emeralds. This may be why emeralds were gifted at significant court events, especially when princes were given new assignments.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/6c2.contextual_description: Inscribed precious stones were a frequent phenomenon encountered at multiple courts across the Islamic world. They were usually inscribed with names of rulers or members of the royal family, court members or noblemen, but also verses of the Quran, depending on the motive of production. Spinels are known to come in a variety of colours, and therefore their use is widespread, and they served as great substitutes for gemstones of the same colour. Due to their glass-like structure, artefacts such as these were great accessories and were even more adored when exposed to light, which enhanced their colour properties.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/ea2.contextual_description: Next to gold, the most precious and praised precious metal is silver. Recognizable by its metallic greyish colour, silver has a multitude of associations and beliefs connected to it. Established as gold’s opposite (in more ways than one), it is commonly associated with the Moon, imitating its reflection and light upon the Earth. For that reason, it was used to create pieces which had spiritual significance, such as pendants, amulets, and bracelets which had important symbols on them. Due to its softness, silver has the possibility to be moulded into any shape and was therefore a great material for creating various forms that were importance for it’ intended wearer(s). It is also associated with powers of protection, particularly from evil spirits and multiple types of demons.

850bc476-a718-531d-afc6-b642074d9598/273.contextual_description: Honorific orders were no exception when it came to lavish decoration in precious metals and stones. Usually decorated with stones of national importance or with stones which were of high quality and praise, we can encounter a large number of military and diplomatic decoration with many colours. With the addition of enamel and precious stones, many national and religious symbols and colours could be included on the pieces, creating a visual representation of the state.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/e7e.contextual_description: Depictions of private life are always of great import as snapshots of times gone by. Furthermore, these scenes give observers a glimpse into the colourful world of houses, palaces, and other private spaces. The painting tells a visual story about the ritual of a young bride preparing for her wedding day. She is distinguishable by her white garments, veil, and rich ornaments, while her female family members gather round and help her. The colours that attribute other figures and details are vibrant, contrasting to white, which symbolises the purity of the bride to be.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/e27.contextual_description: Many researchers from the Western world travelled across the territories of the former Ottoman Empire in order to acquaint themselves with the local traditions and customs of these countries. An intimate and colourful example is one coming from Greece, where a dinner ceremony is depicted. The background is composed of wood like colours, which gives opportunity for the lively coloured figured to stand out and tells the visual story of the customs which take place at the dinner table. The figures are emphasised by varieties of red and blue, as well as contrasting white details bring the colours out even more.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/ac8.contextual_description: This painting, showing the interior of a traditional house in the Boussaada region, elicits a certain intimacy. To further depict the origin and the circumstances of the household, the painter uses blue and yellow to emphasise the garments of the women, since the brushstrokes create an illusion that the colours, figures and background are melting into one entirety.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/ce7.contextual_description: Table sets played an important role in everyday life, especially if guests were invited. Porcelain sets of this kind were commonly used to serve sweets and beverages, and they were usually heavily decorated with bright colours to break the monotony of the standard white colour of porcelain.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/07a.contextual_description: In the case of royalty, it was common that household items in their palaces, villas, and other residences had their initials or coat of arms illustrated on them. This example comes from Portugal during the period of the reign of King Fernando of Saxe Coburg, husband of queen Maria II. The lid bears the king’s monogram “F”, positioned underneath the crown. Pastel floral motifs fill  the areas which are bordered by golden intertwining curves, which give the coffee pot more colour and character. The convex ornaments on the handle and the spout, painted in gold, provide the object with more liveliness and confirm its opulent purpose.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/1cf.contextual_description: Table sets were not only reserved for dining, they were also accompanied by other, smaller dishes for snacks, dried fruits or nuts. Depicting a winter landscape with bare trees, the motifs are of European origin, since many of the Turkish porcelain painters trained in Europe. The landscape is in stark contrast to the monochrome nature of the white porcelain. Additionally, the golden handles and borders indicate the luxurious nature of the objects, as well as bringing more colour to it.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/9b4.contextual_description: Household items were also prone to being created in accordance with the contemporary trends of their time. This example takes its motifs from ancient Egypt, since at the time of production, the construction of the Suez Canal was being undertaken. Since many Europeans associated Egypt with gold due to the great stories about Pharaohs, as well as the objects obtained by museums at the time, household items followed or imitated these colour palettes to embody this cultural phenomenon.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/b99.contextual_description: Objects that can be found within the rooms of wealthy houses, mansions, and palaces are exceptional examples not only of the personal tastes of the owners, but also contemporary influences and fashion.  This sideboard is made out of carved wood inlaid with mother-of-pearl and is a great example of how materials with contrasting colours can create beautiful visual effects on furniture. With the intersection of the overall dark surface of the wood and the bright and reflective mother of pearl, the object gains a more dynamic pattern. Its crowning glory are the extraordinary carvings which further contributes to its beauty.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/270.contextual_description: The main face of the chest is adorned by a composition of flowers, branches and fruits in curvilinear compartments, whilst the corners depict female figures flanked by columns. The interior lid depicts a landscape with five male figures who are scattered across the gentle blue surface. The compositions of fruit and flowers and the soft colours refer to the prevailing influence of the rococo style that was dominant in Greece in the late 18th century.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/28d.contextual_description: Health and self-care have always presented an essential aspect of private life. The way people took care of themselves and their living space said a lot about their financial status, as well as their wellbeing. This example originates from Iran and was destined to be used as a man’s cosmetic case. The women’s bright red drapes and dresses stand out in comparison to the yellow and greenish skin tones and background, yet simultaneously complement them to create a vibrantly coloured piece. Also, this cosmetic case is a nice example of the considerable influence European Baroque painting had on Iranian lacquer work particularly during the Qajar epoch.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/3b6.contextual_description: Even though still life is known as one of the elemental types of painting that demonstrates the technical abilities of a painter, it also gives us a lot of information about the contents of many meals that were being prepared for households across the world. Depicting a plate full of crabs, the vibrant red colour fills the complete composition. The blue and white pitcher, along with the yellow liquid and loaf of bread, attempt to tone down the intensity of the full plate. This kind of arrangement of strong colour presentations distracts the observer from seeing other details within the painting with ease, such as the mouse in the right corner.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/6b5.contextual_description: Food was not the sole thing that painters would incorporate into their still life paintings. Sometimes, these tables would have a variety of everyday items, as well as objects that could give us a deeper understanding of the social status of the household. What is even more insightful about this painting is that it also indicates the season of the year through  its elements and colours. The dead birds indicate the beginning of hunting season, while the choice of fruits alludes to the autumn harvest. The colours are also reminiscent of the season’s colour palette, with yellow, red, orange, and earth tones.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/175.contextual_description: The painting reveals an essential simplicity, in which the central details are the confectionery, pottery and flowers. With the aid of the artist's delicate technique and wide colour palette, the work is transformed into a silent and realistic world of living objects. What is fascinating here is the use of a range of whites which in its subtlety adds to the vivid realism of the painting and heightens the awakening of all five senses that are so evocative of Baroque Art and so characteristic of this artist.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/dfa.contextual_description: Religious life played an equally important role in the private sphere as it did in the public one. Depicting a calligraphic panel, along with a Quran and a bead bracelet, the painter wishes to emphasise the religious character of still life. With the aid of yellow and blue, he brings focus to the centre of the painting, where the calligraphic panel takes the majority of the fictional space, but also the surface of the painting. Other yellow shades fade into the overall background, further pushing the panel into the first plane.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/52e.contextual_description: Paintings which depict the interiors of palaces and villas also provide a lot of information regarding the way people lived, as well as their colourful surroundings. This painting is a great example that illustrates vividly the splendour that could be found inside a palace or fortress belonging to a noble family. The way the walls are decorated in a bright shade of red that extends to even the ceiling of the structure. This design choice illuminates how rich colours and the wealth of a person who owns said property go hand in hand.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/d2d.contextual_description: Paintings which describe the interiors of luxurious palaces and villas are great examples of the display of wealth through art. The scene is also historical because the figures are dressed in a Renaissance style. The focal point of the painting is the heavily golden decorated arch, flanked by arabesques and birds of different colours. This contrast breaks the monochrome nature of the arch and gives literal space for the other elements of the composition. Some of the decorations in the arch were deliberately invented by the artist as the painted wished to further convey the luxury and splendour of the palaces and villas that were erected for the highest levels of society.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/0e4.contextual_description: Orientalist painting, which reached its peak in the 19th century, provided the Western world with an idealised version of how the Orient looked. Through the works of poets, artists, anthropologists, and other researchers, people could have a glimpse at far away worlds and civilisations. An example of a colourful idealistic depiction of the Alhambra palace is this work by Filippo Baratti, where he creates an almost fantasy-like representation of the grand palace. The colours and patterns are exotic, further indicating the Orientalist manner of the work. The two frontal figures are dressed in garments of vibrant colours, which draw attention but do not diminish the rest of the lively coloured background. The primary colours are intertwined to create multiple patterns that fill the canvas, along with green tones to depict the vegetative elements.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/f6b.contextual_description: Except for its panelled wooden ceiling, which has not survived, the room is largely in its original state, with one of the best-preserved painted surfaces—including brilliant pinks, oranges, blues, and greens—of any comparable room of the period. As is characteristic, it is comprised of colourful stone floor tiles, painted and carved wooden walls, elaborate cupboard doors and storage niches. The main floral decoration is likely based on textile designs, while the room’s cornices incorporate detailed depictions of platters of fruit and pastry. The Damascus room is an ideal example of the need for beautiful colours and motifs inside people’s homes.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/e16.contextual_description: The paintings within the Aleppo room thus make up the oldest collection from a Syrian dwelling, dating to the Ottoman period. Since the patron was a Christian, there is a mixture of themes from Islamic and Christian religion. The selection of encircling Psalms, Arabic proverbs and Persian principles further add to the impression of a peaceful community of different religious beliefs living side-by-side. The dominant red colour of the panel frames emphasises the scenes, while the multi coloured ornaments on the frames tone down the intensity of the red. The simultaneous use of primary colours creates a colourful, dynamic, yet coherent whole which tells a story of its own.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/cfb.contextual_description: The miniature house was made by Amy Miles when she was in her thirties, and is made to resemble her childhood home, a large structure consisting of ten rooms. It originally had an artist's studio in the roof. On the ground floor is a child's schoolroom, a small dining room, a kitchen and a pantry. On the next floor is a large and elegant drawing room and a recreation room with a large billiard table. The top floor has a nursery, a bedroom, a bathroom and a utility room. A staircase runs through the centre of the house. This dollhouse is again a great example of the reconstruction of private life, filled with the colours and objects that make a house a home.

a48edfa5-5dbe-57cc-a02c-2487f72e8567/f93.contextual_description: Interiors within the Chigi palace in Ariccia provide a wonderful insight into the private life of noble families in the 16th century. Characterized by vibrant colours which switch between yellow and red, accompanied by lavish paintings and a gold and silver coloured cassette ceiling, the colours bring the interior to life, further contributing to the rich nature of the building and its inhabitants.
